cards.title: Cloud Run Services — Request-Driven Containers
cards.teaser: Cloud Run services run any container that listens on a port, scale from zero to thousands of instances in seconds, and charge only for the CPU and memory consumed while handling requests. This is GCP's primary serverless compute primitive for HTTP workloads.

runs.text: Cloud Run services accept HTTP (or gRPC) traffic and scale automatically based on incoming request volume. The platform manages infrastructure entirely — there are no VMs to configure, no OS patches to apply, and no capacity planning required for typical web workloads.
The canonical deploy command:

items.text: gcloud run deploy my-service --image gcr.io/my-project/my-app:latest --region us-central1 --allow-unauthenticated --port 8080

runs.text: Key flags worth knowing:

items.text: — makes the service publicly accessible. Omit this (the default) to require IAM authentication via a Bearer token.
— keeps at least one instance warm to eliminate cold starts entirely for latency-sensitive endpoints.
— caps horizontal scale to protect downstream databases or third-party API rate limits.
— sets per-instance resource allocation. CPU and memory are always proportional — increasing CPU requires increasing memory.

runs.text: Cloud Run services are
stateless

by design. Any state that needs to survive beyond a single request must live in Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, Firestore, or another external store. The container's local filesystem is ephemeral and is discarded when the instance scales down.
Cloud Run invokes your container over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 on whatever port the container listens on (default 8080, overridable via the PORT environment variable that Cloud Run injects automatically).

Cloud Run services are containers that wake up when a request arrives, handle it, and go back to sleep. You push an image, tell Cloud Run the region, and GCP handles every server concern automatically.

cards.title: Cloud Run Jobs — Batch and Scheduled Container Execution
cards.teaser: Cloud Run jobs run containers to completion rather than waiting for HTTP requests. They are the right tool for batch processing, database migrations, nightly exports, and any task that has a defined end state instead of a persistent listener.

runs.text: Cloud Run
services
and Cloud Run
jobs
share the same underlying infrastructure but serve fundamentally different execution models:

items.text: — long-lived (or zero-to-live) HTTP listeners. Billed per request-second.
— run-to-completion tasks. Billed per CPU/memory second consumed until exit code 0 (success) or non-zero (failure).

runs.text: Creating and executing a job:

items.text: gcloud run jobs create db-migrate --image gcr.io/my-project/migrator:latest --region us-central1 --tasks 1 --max-retries 3
gcloud run jobs execute db-migrate --region us-central1

runs.text: The
--tasks
flag enables parallelism. Setting
--tasks 10
launches 10 container instances in parallel, each receiving a unique
CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX
environment variable (0 through 9). This pattern is ideal for partitioned data processing: each task handles a shard of the input.
Jobs can be triggered on a schedule using Cloud Scheduler (covered in a later card). They do not have a URL endpoint and cannot receive inbound HTTP traffic during execution.
Cloud Run jobs have a maximum execution timeout of 168 hours (7 days), making them suitable for long-running data pipelines that previously required persistent VMs or Cloud Dataflow.
Cloud Run jobs are containers that run, do their work, and exit. Unlike services, they don't wait for HTTP traffic — you trigger them, they finish, and you're billed only for what they used.

cards.title: Cloud Functions 2nd Gen — Event-Driven Functions on Cloud Run
cards.teaser: Cloud Functions 2nd gen is GCP's function-as-a-service offering, rebuilt on top of Cloud Run. This architectural change brings longer timeouts, larger instances, concurrency support, and direct Eventarc integration — eliminating most of 1st gen's practical limitations.

runs.text: Cloud Functions 2nd gen is not a rewrite of the developer experience — you still write a function in Python, Node.js, Go, Java, or Ruby. The difference is the runtime layer underneath: 2nd gen functions compile to container images and run on Cloud Run, while 1st gen used a proprietary sandbox.
Key 2nd gen improvements over 1st gen:

items.text: — up to 60 minutes per invocation (vs. 9 minutes in 1st gen). Enables long-running event handlers.
— up to 32 GB RAM and 8 vCPUs (vs. 8 GB and 4 vCPUs). Suitable for ML inference workloads.
— a single instance can handle up to 1000 concurrent requests (same as Cloud Run). 1st gen was strictly one request per instance.
— native support for CloudEvents from 90+ GCP sources via Eventarc, replacing the bespoke trigger system of 1st gen.

runs.text: Deploying a 2nd gen function:

items.text: gcloud functions deploy my-fn --gen2 --runtime python311 --trigger-http --region us-central1 --entry-point handle_request

runs.text: Because 2nd gen functions run on Cloud Run, you can inspect and manage them in the Cloud Run console. You can also deploy the same container image via either gcloud functions deploy or gcloud run deploy, giving you flexibility on how you author and manage the function.

Cloud Functions 2nd gen is just Cloud Run with a simpler authoring experience and an event trigger model layered on top. You write a function, GCP wraps it in a container, and Eventarc routes events to it.

cards.title: App Engine — Legacy PaaS and When It Still Makes Sense
cards.teaser: App Engine is GCP's original platform-as-a-service, predating Cloud Run by almost a decade. Standard environment scales to zero automatically; Flexible environment runs Docker containers on Compute Engine VMs. Neither is the default choice for new workloads — but understanding both avoids a painful migration later.

runs.text: App Engine has two fundamentally different environments that share a name but almost nothing else:

items.text: — runs in a language-specific sandbox (Python, Java, Go, PHP, Node.js). Scales to zero in milliseconds. No Docker; you deploy source code or a runtime-specific artifact. Strong isolation but restricted file system, no arbitrary binaries, no custom system libraries. Fast cold starts.

— runs Docker containers on Compute Engine VMs managed by App Engine. No scale-to-zero: minimum 1 instance always running, billed by the minute. Supports any runtime and arbitrary binaries. Cold starts are VM-scale (60-120 seconds). Not cost-efficient at low traffic.

runs.text: Comparison with Cloud Run:

items.text: vs. Cloud Run: App Engine Standard has tighter language constraints and a global dispatch routing model (traffic.yaml). Cloud Run is more flexible, supports any container, and has simpler traffic splitting via revision percentages.

vs. Cloud Run: For most containerized workloads, Cloud Run is strictly better — it scales to zero, has no minimum instance cost, and has faster scaling. Flexible is only preferred when App Engine's managed autoscaler and deployment tooling are already deeply embedded in the team's workflow.

runs.text: When App Engine remains the right choice: existing applications already running on App Engine with working deployments and no containerization requirement. Migration risk outweighs the benefits of moving to Cloud Run for stable, low-traffic internal tools.

App Engine applications are scoped to a GCP project, and only one App Engine application can exist per project. You cannot rename or delete a project that has an App Engine app. Factor this into project architecture decisions — it cannot be reversed.

App Engine Standard runs source code in a managed sandbox and scales to zero cheaply; Flexible runs your Docker container on a VM and always keeps one running. For new work, Cloud Run does both jobs better — but App Engine is still running millions of existing apps.

cards.title: Cold Starts — The Serverless Tax
cards.teaser: A cold start is the latency penalty paid when a serverless platform must launch a new container instance to handle a request. Understanding its causes, magnitude, and mitigation strategies is essential for building low-latency Cloud Run services.

runs.text: When Cloud Run needs to scale up — either from zero or when all existing instances are at capacity — it must:

items.text: Pull the container image (or use a cached copy from the nearest image cache).
Execute application initialization code (importing libraries, loading models, establishing database connections).

runs.text: Typical cold start durations: a lightweight Go or Node.js binary with minimal initialization is 50-200ms. A Python service that imports TensorFlow or heavy ML frameworks can take 5-15 seconds. A JVM service that initializes Spring context can take 10-30 seconds.
Cold start mitigation strategies:

items.text: to keep one warm instance always ready. This eliminates cold starts entirely for the initial request at the cost of idle compute billing.
— Cloud Run can temporarily over-provision CPU during container startup. Enable with
flag. Startup is typically 2x faster at no extra charge.
— smaller images pull faster. Use multi-stage Docker builds. Avoid
— defer expensive initialization (database pool creation, model loading) to the first real request rather than doing it at startup. Acceptable if the first-request penalty is tolerable.
— Cloud Run's 2nd gen environment starts faster than 1st gen for most workloads due to full Linux process isolation (no emulation layer).

runs.text: Cloud Run does not cold-start every request to zero — it only cold-starts when it needs to scale up beyond the current instance count. Warm instances handle subsequent requests with no startup overhead. The cold start tax is paid at scale-out events, not per request.

A cold start is the delay between "Cloud Run decides to add a new instance" and "that instance handles its first request." It's proportional to how long your app takes to initialize. Keep images small, initialization fast, and use a warm minimum instance for latency-critical paths.

cards.title: Concurrency Settings — Requests Per Instance
cards.teaser: Cloud Run allows a single container instance to handle multiple requests simultaneously. Setting concurrency correctly is the single most important configuration lever for cost and performance — it determines how many instances Cloud Run actually needs to spin up.

runs.text: Cloud Run's concurrency setting controls the maximum number of simultaneous in-flight requests a single container instance will accept. The default is 80; the maximum is 1000.

How concurrency affects scaling: if your service receives 800 requests per second and each request takes 100ms, that is 80 concurrent requests at any moment. With concurrency=80, one instance handles all of them. With concurrency=1 (1st-gen Cloud Functions behavior), Cloud Run would spawn 80 instances — 80x the cost and 80x the cold-start risk.
Setting concurrency:
When to lower concurrency:

items.text: — if each request saturates a CPU core, high concurrency causes requests to queue behind each other. Lower concurrency forces horizontal scale instead of vertical queuing.
— if each request allocates significant memory (e.g., loading a document into RAM), too many concurrent requests will exhaust the per-instance memory allocation and cause OOM errors.
— applications with shared mutable state that is not thread-safe must use concurrency=1 or refactor the state handling.

runs.text: The rule of thumb: I/O-bound services (database calls, external API calls, file reads) benefit from high concurrency because threads spend most time waiting, not executing. CPU-bound services should target concurrency close to the number of allocated CPU cores.

Cloud Functions 1st gen used concurrency=1 always, which caused cost and cold-start explosions at moderate traffic. Cloud Functions 2nd gen and Cloud Run both default to concurrency=80. If you are migrating from 1st gen, this behavioral change is the most impactful thing to understand.

Concurrency is how many simultaneous requests one instance will accept. High concurrency means fewer instances needed (cheaper, fewer cold starts). Low concurrency means more instances, which is right when each request is CPU-heavy and you don't want them competing for the same core.

cards.title: CPU Allocation Modes — Request-Only vs Always-Allocated
cards.teaser: Cloud Run offers two CPU allocation models that determine when CPU resources are available to the container. Choosing the wrong one causes either wasted billing or background tasks silently dying mid-execution.

runs.text: Cloud Run CPU allocation controls whether CPU is available to the container only during request handling, or continuously while the instance is alive.

items.text: — CPU is throttled to near-zero between requests. The container is "frozen" between invocations. Background goroutines, threads, or async tasks that run after the HTTP response is sent will be killed. Billing stops when the response is returned. This is the lowest-cost mode for pure request/response workloads.

— CPU is available continuously while the instance exists, even between requests. Background tasks, cache warming, WebSocket connections, and streaming responses work correctly. Billed per instance-second, not per request-second. More expensive but required for any workload that does work outside the request/response cycle.

runs.text: Setting CPU allocation:
Common reasons to choose always-allocated:

items.text: Background cache population or metric flushing between requests.
Server-Sent Events (SSE) or WebSocket connections that persist after the initial HTTP upgrade.
that need to do periodic health checks or prefetch data.

runs.text: With CPU-throttling (request-only), even startup code that runs after the initial HTTP response may be interrupted. If your framework runs post-response hooks or deferred cleanup, test carefully — this is a common source of subtle Cloud Run bugs when migrating from always-on server frameworks.

Request-only CPU means your container is frozen between HTTP calls — cheap, but background tasks die. Always-allocated CPU keeps the process truly alive at all times, which costs more but is required for anything beyond pure request/response.

cards.title: Cloud Run gen2 Execution Environment — Full Linux Compatibility
cards.teaser: Cloud Run's second-generation execution environment is a genuine Linux sandbox with full syscall support, network namespaces, and writable local filesystem. It eliminates the behavioral differences that made 1st gen an unreliable host for many container images.

runs.text: Cloud Run gen1 ran containers in a lightweight sandbox derived from gVisor (Google's container security layer). This provided strong isolation but blocked syscalls that standard Linux applications rely on — resulting in containers that worked locally but failed mysteriously on Cloud Run.
Cloud Run gen2 differences:

items.text: — any syscall that works on a standard Linux VM works on gen2. No more mysterious EPERM or ENOSYS errors from filtered system calls.
— each instance gets its own network namespace, enabling use of raw sockets, binding to low-numbered ports, and Unix domain socket communication between processes in the same container.
— gen2 supports writing to local disk, enabling in-process SQLite, local caching, and tools that require writable temp directories.
— gen2 typically has lower cold-start latency because there is no sandbox translation layer between the application and the OS.

runs.text: Enabling gen2:

items.text: gcloud run deploy my-service --execution-environment gen2 --image gcr.io/my-project/my-app

runs.text: gen2 is now the default for new Cloud Run deployments in most regions. It is required for Direct VPC egress (next card) and for Cloud Run functions 2nd gen.

If a container image runs on a standard Docker host but fails on Cloud Run gen1, the fix is almost always to switch to gen2. Rust binaries using io_uring, Go binaries using certain network primitives, and Python packages with native C extensions that issue unusual syscalls are common examples.

gen2 is "real Linux" — your container gets a genuine kernel, full syscall access, and a writable filesystem. gen1 was a sandbox that filtered system calls for security but broke many standard containers. For new deployments, gen2 is the default and the right choice.

cards.title: Direct VPC Egress — Bypass the Serverless VPC Connector
cards.teaser: Direct VPC egress lets Cloud Run containers route traffic directly into a VPC network without the Serverless VPC Connector middleman. It eliminates an entire managed service, reduces latency, and lowers cost for workloads that access private resources like Cloud SQL, Memorystore, or internal APIs.

runs.text: By default, Cloud Run containers cannot reach resources on a private VPC (Cloud SQL via private IP, Memorystore, GKE internal services, on-premises resources via VPN). The original solution was the
Serverless VPC Connector
— a managed cluster of VMs that proxied traffic from serverless products into the VPC. This worked but added cost (always-on VMs), latency (extra hop), and a management surface.
Direct VPC egress removes the connector entirely. With gen2, Cloud Run containers get a network interface directly attached to your VPC subnet, enabling:

items.text: Private IP connectivity to Cloud SQL, Memorystore (Redis/Memcached), and internal load balancers.
VPC firewall rule enforcement at the instance level (not at a proxy).
Reduced latency — one fewer hop vs. Serverless VPC Connector.
No connector scaling or sizing concerns.

runs.text: Enabling direct VPC egress:

items.text: gcloud run deploy my-service --network my-vpc --subnet my-subnet --vpc-egress all-traffic --execution-environment gen2

runs.text: The
--vpc-egress all-traffic
flag routes all outbound traffic through the VPC (enabling a NAT gateway for controlled internet egress). Use
--vpc-egress private-ranges-only
to route only RFC 1918 addresses through VPC while sending public traffic directly.

Direct VPC egress requires gen2 execution environment and a VPC subnet with sufficient IP address space — Cloud Run allocates one IP per instance. Ensure your subnet CIDR is sized for your maximum instance count, not just your steady-state.

Direct VPC egress plugs Cloud Run directly into your private network. Before this, you needed a VPC Connector (a middleman cluster of VMs). Now your Cloud Run instance gets its own IP on the subnet, talks to Cloud SQL or Redis directly, and the connector is gone.

cards.title: Cloud Scheduler — Cron-Style Triggers
cards.teaser: Cloud Scheduler is GCP's managed cron service. It sends HTTP, Pub/Sub, or App Engine HTTP requests on a cron schedule, making it the standard trigger mechanism for Cloud Run jobs, Cloud Functions, and Cloud Run services that need scheduled invocation.

runs.text: Cloud Scheduler manages fully-hosted cron jobs. It handles timezone-aware scheduling, guaranteed delivery with configurable retry policies, and target delivery to three endpoint types:

items.text: — sends an HTTP request to any URL (Cloud Run services, Cloud Functions, external webhooks). Supports auth headers (OIDC or OAuth2 tokens for GCP-authenticated endpoints).
— publishes a message to a Pub/Sub topic, which triggers any downstream subscriber (Cloud Functions, Dataflow, etc.).
— dedicated target for App Engine Standard services with built-in IAM integration.

runs.text: Creating a scheduler job to trigger a Cloud Run job every night at 2 AM UTC:

items.text: gcloud scheduler jobs create http nightly-export --schedule "0 2 * * *" --uri "https://us-central1-run.googleapis.com/apis/run.googleapis.com/v1/namespaces/my-project/jobs/db-export:run" --http-method POST --oauth-service-account-email scheduler-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com --location us-central1

runs.text: The service account must have the
run.jobs.run
permission on the Cloud Run job (granted by the
Cloud Run Invoker
role). Cloud Scheduler will request an OIDC token for the service account and attach it as a Bearer header.

Cloud Scheduler guarantees at-least-once delivery. For idempotent jobs this is fine. For jobs that must not run twice (e.g., financial settlements), implement idempotency keys or use Cloud Tasks with deduplication IDs instead.

Cloud Scheduler is cron-as-a-service. Give it a cron expression, a target (HTTP URL, Pub/Sub topic, or App Engine), and it fires the trigger on schedule. It handles retries, auth, and timezone awareness so you don't have to run a VM just to run a cron job.

cards.title: Cloud Tasks — Async Work Queue
cards.teaser: Cloud Tasks is GCP's managed task queue for dispatching asynchronous work. It provides durable enqueuing, rate limiting, retry policies, and deduplication — decoupling producers from consumers in ways that direct HTTP calls and Pub/Sub cannot.

runs.text: Cloud Tasks solves a specific distributed systems problem: you want to enqueue a unit of work to be executed later (or at a specific time) with reliable delivery, controlled throughput, and retries on failure — without coupling the enqueuer to the executor.
Core Cloud Tasks concepts:

items.text: — a named, configured buffer. Each queue has a
cap. Use per-queue rate limits to protect downstream services from being overwhelmed.
— an HTTP request payload enqueued to a queue. When dispatched, Cloud Tasks POSTs the payload to the configured handler URL (a Cloud Run service, Cloud Function, or any HTTPS endpoint).
in the future, making Cloud Tasks a reliable delayed-execution mechanism (e.g., "send this email in 10 minutes if the user hasn't verified").
prevents duplicate enqueuing within a 4-day deduplication window. Critical for exactly-once semantics in payment or notification systems.

runs.text: Cloud Tasks vs Pub/Sub:

items.text: when you need: per-task scheduling, rate-limited dispatch, explicit deduplication, or the ability to delete an enqueued task before it runs.
when you need: fan-out to multiple subscribers, filter-based routing, streaming semantics, or integrations with Dataflow/BigQuery.

runs.text: Cloud Tasks retries failed tasks with exponential backoff. The handler must return HTTP 2xx to acknowledge success. A 4xx response signals a permanent failure (task is discarded). A 5xx or network timeout triggers a retry up to the queue's configured maxAttempts.

Cloud Tasks is a durable to-do list. You add tasks to a queue; Cloud Tasks delivers them to your handler at a controlled rate with retries on failure. Unlike Pub/Sub, you can schedule tasks in the future, deduplicate them, and delete them before they fire.

cards.title: Eventarc — Event-Driven Integration Backbone
cards.teaser: Eventarc is GCP's unified event routing service. It connects over 90 Google Cloud event sources to Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, and GKE using the CloudEvents standard — replacing the bespoke trigger systems of older GCP services with a single, consistent model.

runs.text: Before Eventarc, different GCP services had different event delivery mechanisms: Cloud Functions had its own trigger system, Cloud Run had no native event routing, and integrations between GCP services required hand-written Pub/Sub plumbing. Eventarc standardizes all of this.
Eventarc event sources include:

items.text: — any admin or data access audit log entry from any GCP service. This is the most flexible source: it fires on almost any GCP API operation (e.g., "a BigQuery table was created", "a Cloud SQL instance was deleted").
— Cloud Storage (object finalized/deleted), Pub/Sub (message published), Cloud Build (build completed), Firebase, and many others emit CloudEvents directly without requiring Audit Log routing.
— Eventarc can route any Pub/Sub message as a CloudEvent, bridging non-native sources.

runs.text: Creating an Eventarc trigger:

items.text: gcloud eventarc triggers create gcs-upload-trigger --destination-run-service my-processor --destination-run-region us-central1 --event-filters type=google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized --event-filters bucket=my-uploads --location us-central1 --service-account eventarc-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

runs.text: Eventarc delivers events as
CloudEvents

(the CNCF standard). Your Cloud Run handler receives a structured JSON envelope with event metadata (source, type, subject, time) plus the event-specific data payload. This portability means the same handler logic can be tested locally with a curl command using a fabricated CloudEvent.

Eventarc delivers events at-least-once with a configurable retry window (default 24 hours, max 7 days). Handlers must be idempotent. The CloudEvent id field is the deduplication key — store processed event IDs in Firestore or Cloud Spanner if exactly-once processing is required.

Eventarc is the event bus that wires GCP services together. When a file lands in Cloud Storage, Eventarc notices, wraps it in a CloudEvent, and delivers it to your Cloud Run service or function. You define the filter; Eventarc handles routing, delivery, and retries.

cards.title: Cloud Workflows — Orchestration of GCP Services
cards.teaser: Cloud Workflows is GCP's managed orchestration engine. It sequences calls to GCP APIs, HTTP endpoints, and custom connectors with conditional logic, error handling, parallel branches, and durable state — replacing fragile shell-script orchestration or ad-hoc chaining through Pub/Sub.

runs.text: Cloud Workflows uses a YAML or JSON workflow definition language to describe multi-step processes. Unlike Pub/Sub chaining (where each service triggers the next) or Cloud Composer (Apache Airflow, oriented toward data pipelines), Workflows is designed for API orchestration: coordinating multiple GCP services into a single logical operation with full error handling.
A minimal workflow that calls a Cloud Run service, stores the result, then calls a second service:

items.text:
main:
  steps:
    - step1:
        call: http.post
        args:
          url: https://my-service-xxxx.run.app/process
          body:
            input: ${sys.get_env("GOOGLE_CLOUD_WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_ID")}
        result: step1Result
    - step2:
        call: http.post
        args:
          url: https://notify-service-xxxx.run.app/notify
          body:
            result: ${step1Result.body}
        result: step2Result
    - done:
        return: ${step2Result.body}

runs.text: Cloud Workflows key capabilities:

items.text: — workflow state persists across GCP infrastructure failures. A step that times out is retried; a completed step is never re-executed.
step type fans out multiple sub-steps and waits for all to complete before continuing.
— pre-built call connectors for BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Firestore, Secret Manager, and 60+ other GCP services. No manual HTTP construction or auth token management needed.
— a workflow can pause and wait for an external event (e.g., a human approval) via a callback endpoint, resuming when the callback is invoked.

runs.text: Cloud Workflows vs Cloud Composer: Composer (Airflow) is oriented toward data pipelines with DAGs, scheduled batch processing, and Python-native operators. Workflows is lighter, serverless (no cluster to manage), and better suited to API orchestration, microservice coordination, and event-driven processes.

Workflows executions are billed per step (not per second), making them extremely cost-efficient for low-frequency orchestration. A workflow with 10 steps running 1000 times per month costs less than a dollar. There is no charge for a workflow that sits idle waiting for a callback.

Cloud Workflows is a durable script that calls GCP APIs and HTTP endpoints in a defined order with if-this-then-that logic, retries, and parallel branches. Think of it as replacing a bash script that chains GCP commands — except it survives failures, never double-executes a completed step, and has no server to manage.
